modules.name: Albert Adu Boahen
modules.outcome: Re-read a colonial-period claim from the African side: what did Africans do, and what lasted?
modules.intro: Boahen (1932 to 2006) was a Ghanaian historian who made African perspectives central to the study of the colonial period. Here we borrow one habit of his: ask what Africans were doing, and what continued.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read an encyclopaedic page in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says he taught at the University of Ghana from 1959 to 1990, was professor from 1971, was the first African to chair its history department, and worked on the UNESCO General History of Africa committee from 1993 to 1999. {{wiki-boahen}}
Our library cites his view that the colonial period was short and that African institutions persisted. We did not read his books, so the method below is our application, not his words. {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: Start from the African actors. Name who acted, for example Menelik at Adwa. {{lib}}
Ask what continued under colonial rule: chiefs, markets, languages, institutions. {{lib}}
Ask what the colonial sources leave out, as Iliffe noted of the German history of Maji Maji. {{wiki-maji}}
Compare the colonial record with an African voice, such as oral testimony or a memoir. {{lib}}
Tag the result and say which perspective you used.

modules.name: W. E. B. Du Bois
modules.outcome: Combine evidence with organising: ask what a document shows, and who gathered it and for what purpose.
modules.intro: Du Bois (1868 to 1963) was a scholar and organiser who convened the Pan-African Congresses. Here we borrow his twin habit: collect the data, then argue from it, which is also the habit that exposes a fake.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read an encyclopaedic page in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says his first major academic work, The Philadelphia Negro (1899), was a detailed sociological study based on fieldwork in 1896 and 1897. His 1935 Black Reconstruction marshalled extensive references. He co-founded the NAACP in 1909. {{wiki-dubois}}
He moved to Ghana in October 1961 and died in Accra on 27/08/1963, aged 95, and was given a state funeral. Our library names him as organiser of the Pan-African Congresses. {{wiki-dubois}} {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: Ask what data supports the claim, as in his fieldwork. {{wiki-dubois}}
Ask for references, as in Black Reconstruction. {{wiki-dubois}}
Ask who organised the evidence and why. {{lib}}
Run the four tests of authenticity on any quoted document.
Say plainly what the evidence supports and what it does not.

modules.name: Julius Nyerere
modules.outcome: Judge an independence project by its own stated aim and by its results, and name a criterion first.
modules.intro: Nyerere (1922 to 1999) led Tanganyika to independence and proclaimed ujamaa. We borrow one habit: state the aim, then test results against it, and admit the costs.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read an encyclopaedic page in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says he was born on 13/04/1922 and died on 14/10/1999, helped form TANU in 1954 and campaigned for independence, and was influenced by Gandhi to preach non-violent protest. It says his ideology, ujamaa, was a form of African socialism, and that he developed much of his philosophy while studying in Edinburgh. {{wiki-nyerere}}
He also translated Shakespeare's Julius Caesar and The Merchant of Venice into Swahili. Our library records that he stepped down voluntarily in 1985. {{wiki-nyerere}} {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: State the aim: self-reliance, villages, equality. {{lib}}
List results: literacy, unity and no ethnic civil war. {{lib}}
List costs: compulsory villagisation and falling output. {{lib}}
Choose a criterion and say why.
State the limit of your evidence.

modules.name: Steve Biko
modules.outcome: Separate the system from the mind: ask what a law did, and what it asked people to believe about themselves.
modules.intro: Biko (1946 to 1977) was the leading voice of Black Consciousness. We borrow one habit: define terms precisely and ask what a system did to people's sense of themselves.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read an encyclopaedic page in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says Biko was born on 18/12/1946, founded the South African Students' Organisation in 1968 and helped develop its Black Consciousness ideology. A 1971 SASO manifesto, as reported, defined it as an attitude of mind and a way of life. {{wiki-biko}}
He was banned in 1973 and arrested in August 1977, and died on 12/09/1977 after beatings in police custody. In 2025 the National Prosecuting Authority said it would reopen the inquest. {{wiki-biko}}
His method, step by step

i: Define each term before using it: law, policy, event. {{lib}}
Ask what a measure did to movement, housing or schooling. {{lib}}
Ask what it asked people to accept about themselves.
Ask who gained from the category.
Keep the evidence of what happened apart from the interpretation.

modules.name: Chinua Achebe
modules.outcome: Read a witness and a historian together, and mark which questions each can answer.
modules.intro: Achebe (1930 to 2013) was a Nigerian novelist who served Biafra as an envoy. We borrow one habit: place the witness beside the numbers, and say what each adds and what each lacks.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read an encyclopaedic page in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says he was born on 16/11/1930 and died on 21/03/2013, published Things Fall Apart in 1958, travelled as an ambassador promoting the Biafran cause, and published There Was a Country in 2012, a work that reopened discussion of the Nigerian civil war. {{wiki-achebe}}
The page also notes that critics have called him sexist in his depiction of Igbo society, which is a reminder that every witness has limits. We did not read his books. {{wiki-achebe}} {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: Read the witness for what it was like to live through the event.
Read the historian for scale and cause. {{lib}}
Mark where they agree and where they conflict.
Mark what each lacks.
Do not use the witness for a number, or the number for the experience.

modules.name: Julius Nyerere
modules.outcome: Judge an institution against its founding aim and against what members were willing to give up.
modules.intro: Nyerere preferred gradual steps to unity over a continental government. We apply that stance to the African Union and ask what states were willing to give up.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read an encyclopaedic page in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia reports that he published widely, wrote poetry and developed his ujamaa ideology. Our library records that in the 1960s he and others preferred gradual regional steps to Nkrumah's continental government. {{wiki-nyerere}} {{lib}}
Confidence: partial. The application to the AU is our inference, not a quotation from him. {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: State the founding aim of the institution. {{lib}}
List what members agreed to give up.
Compare words with practice: Article 4(h) against money and reluctance. {{lib}}
Ask whether gradual steps or a single leap fits better.
State the limit of the evidence.
